opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the fundamental issue is one of representation. Deep learning systems are, at bottom, circuits: very large, very flexible circuits, but circuits nonetheless. And circuits are a remarkably poor way to represent certain kinds of knowledge. If you think about something like the rules of Go, you can write those down in a page or so of first-order logic or a program. But to represent the same thing as a circuit, you need something enormous, and even then the network doesn't really learn the rules. It learns a huge collection of approximations that work most of the time in the regions of the space it's seen.

We actually saw this quite concretely with the Go programs that were supposed to be superhuman. It turned out that relatively weak amateur players, using strategies found by adversarial search, could beat them, because the programs had never properly grasped the concept of a group of stones being connected and alive or dead. A human beginner gets that concept in a few minutes. The network, after millions of games, didn't have it in any general form. To me, that's a very telling sign. It suggests these systems are not acquiring the kind of compact, generalizable knowledge we'd expect from something that truly understands the domain.

The same issue shows up in sample efficiency. Humans can learn from one or two examples, or even from being told something in words, because we have expressive representations and lots of prior knowledge we can bring to bear. Deep learning systems typically need vast amounts of data, and much of that need comes from the mismatch between the representation and the structure of the world.

Then there's the question of reasoning and planning over long time scales. The real world requires managing activity at many levels of abstraction: deciding to write a paper, then structuring an argument, then choosing words, then moving your fingers. We do this hierarchically, and we construct those abstractions ourselves. I don't see much evidence that deep learning, as it currently stands, is discovering such hierarchies in a robust way. Large language models can produce text that looks like planning, but when you probe them on genuinely novel problems, the cracks show.

So I'm not saying deep learning is useless, far from it. It's been an extraordinary tool for perception and for certain pattern-recognition tasks. But I think it will turn out to be one component of a larger picture, and that we'll need to bring back ideas from probabilistic programming, from logic, from structured representations, and combine them with learning. The idea that we can just scale up circuits and get general intelligence out the other end strikes me as, at best, an unproven bet, and at worst a way of building systems we don't understand and therefore can't trust.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limits of deep learning in representation, sample efficiency, and planning, but does not identify end-to-end factory design as an inapplicable task.

r002.rationale: The response does not argue that important problems are ignored within AI because deep learning has nothing to contribute; it instead describes deep learning as useful in some areas and proposes combining it with other approaches.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that deep learning has been enormously successful, and I don't want to minimize that. Perception tasks in particular, vision, speech recognition, those have been transformed. But I think there's a tendency to extrapolate from those successes to the idea that if we just keep scaling up the data and the compute, we'll get to general intelligence, and I don't think that follows.

The fundamental issue, as I see it, is that a deep network is essentially a very large circuit. It's a function from inputs to outputs, and circuits are a fairly impoverished representation. They don't have a natural way to express things like "all the objects in the room" or "for every person, there is some person who is their mother." Those are quantified, relational, compositional statements, and we've known since the early days of computer science that you can't express them concisely in a circuit. You end up needing exponentially large circuits to represent what could be stated in one line of first-order logic or a few lines of a probabilistic program. So when people say "we'll just learn that from data," they're asking the network to rediscover, from examples, structure that would be essentially impossible to represent in that form in the first place.

That shows up practically in a few places. One is data efficiency. Humans learn from very few examples because we bring prior knowledge, we bring an understanding of how the world is put together, and deep learning typically doesn't. A child doesn't need ten million labeled images to recognize a giraffe. The second is reasoning over long horizons. Planning, where you have to think many steps ahead and consider the consequences of actions, is something that classical AI handled with explicit models and search, and deep learning on its own really struggles with it. You see that in things like the chess and Go programs, where the deep network is doing evaluation but the actual lookahead is still a tree search that someone wrote by hand. The third is what I'd call knowledge accumulation. If I tell you a fact, you incorporate it immediately and can use it in novel ways. A deep network trained end to end doesn't have a mechanism for that, short of retraining.

So my view is that the next phase of progress is going to come from combining the pattern recognition strengths of deep learning with the expressive representations and reasoning capabilities from the rest of AI, probabilistic programming, logical reasoning, and so on. There's a lot of excellent work in that direction. I think the people who believe deep learning alone is the whole story are going to be disappointed, and the people who think it has no role are also going to be wrong. The interesting territory is in between.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limits in representation, data efficiency, planning, and knowledge accumulation, but does not identify end-to-end factory design as an unsuitable task.

r002.rationale: The response does not argue that important AI problems are ignored because deep learning has nothing to contribute. It says deep learning has important strengths and that the view it has no role is wrong.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we have to distinguish between deep learning as a way of representing and learning functions, which is tremendously useful, and the idea that it provides a complete approach to intelligence.

One limitation is that many problems require you to reason over a variable number of objects and relationships. If I tell you that every person has a mother, and then ask about the mother of someone you’ve never heard of, you can apply that knowledge immediately. You don’t need thousands of examples involving that particular person. We want systems that can express general knowledge and apply it in new circumstances, reliably.

Another issue is making decisions over long time horizons. Suppose you want to organize a conference, or build a house. You reason at different levels of abstraction, break the task into pieces, and work out how those pieces depend on each other. Learning a direct mapping from observations to actions doesn’t, by itself, explain how to do that.

That doesn’t mean neural networks can’t contribute to reasoning or planning. They certainly can. But the fact that a network can represent a solution is very different from saying that we have a practical method for learning that solution, with a reasonable amount of data and computation. That gap is where a lot of the important questions lie.

r001.rationale: The response discusses planning tasks such as organizing a conference or building a house, but does not identify end-to-end factory design as a task deep learning cannot handle.

r002.rationale: The response does not argue that important problems are ignored because deep learning has nothing to contribute; it explicitly says neural networks can contribute to reasoning and planning.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think we have to distinguish between deep learning as a way of representing functions and deep learning as a way of building intelligent systems. Neural networks are very expressive. But that doesn't mean that training a large network on examples gives you all the capabilities you need for intelligence.

One important issue is the ability to reason about things you haven't seen before. If I describe a new game to you, you can understand the rules and start thinking about how to play. You don't need to watch a million games first. You can use a description of the world to work out the consequences of actions. Learning can certainly help with that, but it doesn't replace the need for reasoning and planning.

Another issue is that, in the real world, you don't get to specify every possible situation in the training data. You need systems that can combine what they know, recognize what they don't know, and sometimes ask for information. Being very good at predicting an output from an input is useful, but it's only part of that picture.

So I wouldn't say there's some simple boundary beyond which neural networks cannot go. I'd say that we shouldn't confuse the success of a particular learning method with having solved the whole problem of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify end-to-end factory design or say deep learning is inapplicable to it.

r002.rationale: It discusses limits of deep learning, but does not argue that important AI problems are ignored because deep learning has nothing to contribute to them.
